claims.text: The catalytic performance of Pt-based nanoscale catalysts for ethanol oxidation is governed by the adsorption energies of key reaction intermediates.
Controlled alloying can tune intermediate binding by changing the local electronic environment.
Appropriately tuned binding enables efficient electron and proton transfer while avoiding poisoning or overbinding.
The baseline is a nanoscale catalyst primarily composed of Pt with a well-defined surface structure.
Adding a controlled amount of a second metal will alter the local electronic structure of Pt sites.
Adding a second metal will induce surface strain.
DFT can identify alloy compositions having near-optimal adsorption energies for ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
The comparison will be conducted for ethanol oxidation under alkaline conditions at moderate temperature, using pure Pt as the baseline.
Alloying causes changes in electronic structure and strain at active Pt sites that alter intermediate adsorption energies.
Adsorption energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates, including acetaldehyde- and acetic-acid-related fragments, control electron and proton transfer.
Overstabilized ethanol-oxidation intermediates act as poisoning species.
Tuning adsorption energies through alloying promotes intermediate transformation and prevents active-site blockage.
Balancing adsorption energies will enhance catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability.
The alloy catalyst will have a lower onset potential, higher current density, and improved durability than pure Pt.
In situ spectroscopy will show that adsorption energies shift toward DFT-predicted optimal values.
The proposed mechanism should apply primarily to catalysts with similar nanoscale morphology under alkaline, moderate-temperature conditions where electronic and strain effects dominate.
Extreme composition changes or different reaction media may obscure the relationship between adsorption energies and performance.
DFT predicts adsorption-energy trends, but the magnitude of energy shifts and their quantitative effects on catalytic metrics are uncertain.
Particle-size distribution and catalyst-support interactions may also affect the measured outcomes.

The hypothesis is falsified if catalysts with DFT-predicted near-optimal adsorption energies fail to outperform pure Pt significantly, or if predicted non-optimal catalysts outperform predicted optimal catalysts.
